title: Strangers in the rule
hook: a small practice of welcome: Abraham ran from his tent door to meet three strangers, and the rabbis called welcoming guests greater than receiving God's presence
tomorrow: why would giving the money away be called the true bargain?

segments.voice: The hard ones: Beruriah said pray for the sins to end, not the sinners. From the people we know too well to the people we don't know at all.
screen: `THE HARD ONES.` → `PEOPLE WE DON'T KNOW AT ALL.`

segments.voice: It's possible to know a delivery driver's car better than a neighbor's name. Abraham is sitting in the door of his tent, in the plains of Mamre, "in the heat of the day." The hour when nobody moves. The Torah says the LORD appeared to him there. And then: "he lift up his eyes and looked, and, lo, three men stood by him: and when he saw them, he ran to meet them from the tent door."
screen: `A NEIGHBOR'S NAME.` → `THE HEAT OF THE DAY.` → `THREE MEN STAND BY HIM.` → `HE RAN TO MEET THEM.`

segments.voice: An old man, running, in the heat, toward people he doesn't know. He bows. He begs them to stay: let a little water be fetched to wash your feet, rest under the tree, I'll bring a morsel of bread. Then he hurries to Sarah to bake cakes, runs to the herd for a calf, and stands by them under the tree while they eat. A morsel, he said. He brought a feast. The strangers turn out to be messengers, carrying the news that Sarah will have a son. Christians hear this scene in a New Testament line: "Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares." The rabbis drew a Jewish teaching from it. The LORD had appeared to Abraham, and Abraham left that moment to run to the guests. So the Talmud says it outright: welcoming guests is greater than receiving the Divine Presence. Jews call it hachnasat orchim, bringing in guests. A stranger in the rule doesn't need a feast. It starts with the running: noticing first, moving first, offering the morsel.
screen: `A MORSEL, AND THEN A FEAST.` · `ANGELS UNAWARES.` · `GREATER THAN GOD'S PRESENCE.` · `HACHNASAT ORCHIM: BRINGING IN GUESTS.` · then, large: `THE STRANGER.`

segments.voice: Sit facing a door, if you can, the way Abraham sat in his tent door. Let your hands rest open on your knees. Bring to mind one person you pass but have never welcomed, and choose the first small thing you'd offer.
Strangers in the rule: a small practice of welcome, written into your rule, moving first toward people you don't know, the way Abraham ran from his tent door.
Take this with you: the stranger. He promised a morsel and ran to bring a feast. Day 1660, and the door's open.

howItsDone: Jews call welcoming guests hachnasat orchim and trace it to Abraham at Mamre. Christians read the same scene with Hebrews 13:2. Some people write one small act of welcome for strangers into their rule.
